{82} As for the wall: that which I set upright, ﴿it belonged to two orphan boys in the town, and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them, and their father had been righteous﴾; that is, their situation called for compassion and mercy toward them, because they were young and had lost their father, and God also preserved them through the righteousness of their father. ﴿So your Lord willed that they reach maturity and extract their treasure﴾; that is, for this reason I tore down the wall, extracted what was beneath it of their treasure, returned it to them, and rebuilt it without payment. ﴿As a mercy from your Lord﴾; that is, what I did was a mercy from God, which God gave to His servant al-Khidr. ﴿And I did not do it of my own accord﴾; that is, I did not do anything on my own initiative or by my own mere will, but it was from God's mercy and His command. ﴿That is the interpretation of that about which you could not have patience﴾: which I have explained to you.

In this wondrous and noble story there are many benefits, rulings and principles, and we will point out some of them, with God's help:

Among them: the virtue of knowledge and of journeying in its pursuit, and that it is among the most important matters. Musa (peace be upon him) traveled a long distance, suffered weariness in seeking it, and left off sitting with the Children of Israel to teach and guide them, choosing travel to increase his knowledge over that.

Among them: beginning with the more important and then the more important: increasing knowledge and a person's own knowledge is more important than abandoning that and occupying oneself with teaching without having provided oneself with knowledge; combining both is more complete.

Among them: the permissibility of taking a servant both at home and while traveling, to meet needs and seek comfort, as Musa did.

Among them: that the traveler seeking knowledge, or jihad, or something similar, if the benefit requires informing others of his purpose and where he intends to go, then this is more complete than concealing it; for in making it known there are benefits: preparing its provisions, undertaking the matter with insight, and showing longing for this noble act of worship, as Musa said: ﴿I will not give up until I reach the meeting place of the two seas, or I will journey on for years﴾; and as the Prophet (ﷺ) informed his companions when he marched to Tabuk, stating his direction openly, although his habit was to use indirect speech; and that was in accordance with what benefits.

Among them: attributing evil and its causes to Satan, in the sense of enticement and adornment, although everything is by God's decree and determination, as in the statement of Musa's servant: ﴿And none caused me to forget it except Satan, that I should mention it﴾.

Among them: the permissibility of a person reporting what is part of the nature of the soul, such as weariness, hunger or thirst, when it is not in the manner of complaining bitterly and is truthful; as in Musa's statement: ﴿We have indeed suffered weariness from this journey of ours﴾.

Among them: the recommendation that a person's servant be clever, perceptive and shrewd, so that the matter he intends may be accomplished for him.

Among them: the recommendation that a person feed his servant from his own food, and that they eat together; for the apparent meaning of his words ﴿Bring us our morning meal﴾, attributing it to all of them, is that he and his servant both ate.

Among them: that help descends upon the servant according to his fulfilling what he is commanded, and that one who complies with God's command is helped in ways that others are not helped; as in His statement ﴿We have indeed suffered weariness from this journey of ours﴾, referring to the journey beyond the meeting place of the two seas. As for the first journey, they did not complain of weariness during it despite its length, because it was the true journey. As for the last one, it apparently lasted part of a day, because they lost the fish when they took refuge at the rock; so apparently they spent the night there, then they set out the next day, until when it came time for the morning meal, Musa said to his servant: ﴿Bring us our morning meal﴾; then he remembered that he had forgotten it at the place which was the end of his goal.

Among them: that this servant whom they met was not a prophet, but a righteous servant; for He described him with servanthood, and mentioned God's favor upon him with mercy and knowledge, and did not mention his messengership or prophethood; and had he been a prophet, that would have been mentioned as it was mentioned for others. As for his statement at the end of the story: ﴿And I did not do it of my own accord﴾, it does not indicate that he was a prophet, but indicates inspiration and being spoken to by God, as is the case for non-prophets, as God, exalted be He, said: ﴿And We inspired the mother of Musa: suckle him﴾, and ﴿Your Lord inspired the bee: take for yourself houses in the mountains﴾.

Among them: that knowledge which God teaches His servants is of two kinds: acquired knowledge, which the servant attains through his diligence and effort; and a kind of knowledge given directly from God (ladunni), which God bestows on whom He favors among His servants; as in His statement: ﴿And We taught him knowledge from Our presence﴾.

Among them: courtesy toward the teacher, and that the student addresses him in the gentlest manner; as in the words of Musa (peace be upon him): ﴿May I follow you on condition that you teach me of what you have been taught, as guidance?﴾. He phrased his speech in a manner of gentleness and consultation: whether you permit me in that or not. And his acknowledgment that he is learning from him, unlike the case of those who are rude or proud, who do not show the teacher their need for his knowledge, but claim that they cooperate with him, and may even think that they are teaching their teacher while being utterly ignorant. Humbling oneself before the teacher and showing one's need to be taught is among the most beneficial things for the student.

Among them: the humility of the superior person in learning from one who is below him; for Musa was without doubt superior to al-Khidr.

Among them: the learning of a superior scholar in a field in which he has not mastered from one who has mastered it, even if the latter is below him in knowledge by many degrees; for Musa (peace be upon him) was among the ulu al-'azm (steadfast resolute messengers), whom God granted and gave knowledge that He gave to no one else; but in this specific knowledge, al-Khidr had what Musa did not have. Therefore he eagerly sought to learn from him. On this basis, it is not appropriate for a jurist or hadith scholar who is deficient in the science of grammar (nahw), morphology (sarf), or similar disciplines to refrain from learning them from one who has mastered them, even if he himself is not a hadith scholar or jurist.

Among them: attributing knowledge and other virtues to God, the Exalted, acknowledging that, and thanking God for them; as in His statement ﴿that you teach me of what you have been taught﴾; that is, of what God, the Exalted, has taught you.

Among them: that beneficial knowledge is knowledge that guides to good. Every knowledge that contains guidance and direction to the path of good, and warning against the path of evil or a means to that, is beneficial knowledge. Anything beyond that is either harmful or has no benefit; as in His statement ﴿that you teach me of what you have been taught, as guidance﴾.

Among them: that whoever lacks the strength of patience in keeping company with a scholar and with knowledge, and lacks steadfastness in that, will lose much of the knowledge in proportion to his lack of patience. Whoever lacks patience does not attain knowledge, and whoever employs patience and persists in it attains through it every matter he strives for. This is shown by al-Khidr's statement, excusing himself to Musa by mentioning the obstacle that prevents Musa from learning from him: that he would not be able to remain patient with him.

Among them: that a major cause of attaining patience is a person's comprehensive knowledge and experience of the matter for which he has been commanded to be patient; otherwise, one who does not understand it, or does not understand its end, result, benefit or fruit, does not possess the cause of patience. This is shown by His statement ﴿And how can you have patience about that which you do not encompass in knowledge?﴾; so He made the reason for his lack of patience his failure to comprehend the matter in knowledge.

Among them: the command to be deliberate and careful, and not to rush to judge a thing until one knows what is intended by it and what its purpose is.

Among them: making future actions that depend on human choice conditional upon God's will, and that a person should not say of something: "I will do that in the future," except by saying "God willing."

Among them: that resolving to do something is not the same as doing it; for Musa said: ﴿You will find me, God willing, patient﴾.

Then he resolved to be patient, but he did not do so.

Among its lessons: when the teacher sees that it is in the student's interest to be restrained from beginning to ask about certain matters, so that the teacher is the one who brings him to them, then the teacher may do so, since benefit follows what is best. This applies, for example, when the student's understanding is limited, or when the teacher forbids him from probing into matters whose importance is less than others, or matters his mind cannot grasp, or when he asks a question that is not relevant to the subject under discussion.

Among its lessons: it is permissible to board the sea in circumstances other than those in which one fears for one's safety.

Among its lessons: the one who forgets is not held accountable for his forgetting, neither in respect of the rights of God nor in respect of the rights of people, since He said: ﴿Do not hold me accountable for what I forgot﴾.

Among its lessons: a person should take from people's characters and dealings what is easy and what they willingly give, and he should not burden them with what they cannot bear or what would be hard and oppressive for them, for this leads to aversion and weariness. Rather, he should take what is readily available, so that the matter becomes easy for him.

Among its lessons: matters are judged by their outward appearance, and worldly rulings concerning property, blood and other things depend upon it. Moses (peace be upon him) objected to al-Khidr's damaging of the boat and killing of the boy, and these matters outwardly appear to be wrongful. Moses (peace be upon him) could not remain silent about them in circumstances other than those in which he accompanied al-Khidr. So he was hasty, rushed to judgment according to their general state, and did not heed this incidental factor which obliged him to be patient and not to hasten to object.

Among its lessons: the great and sublime principle (qa'idah) that a greater evil is averted by committing a lesser evil, and the greater of two benefits is preserved by forgoing the lesser of them. The killing of the boy was an evil, but his remaining alive until he tempted his parents away from their religion was a greater evil than that, and his remaining alive without being killed and preserved, even if one supposes it to be good, is less good than preserving his parents' religion and their faith. Therefore al-Khidr killed him. Under this principle there are branches and benefits that cannot be enumerated, and the clashing of all benefits and harms falls under it.

Among its lessons: another great principle, namely that a person's action concerning another's property, when done for the sake of benefit and removing harm, is permissible, even without permission, and even if his action results in the destruction of part of another's property. Just as al-Khidr damaged the boat so that it would be defective and thus be safe from the seizure of the oppressive king. Accordingly: if a fire, a flood or something similar occurs in a person's house or property, and the destruction of some of the property or the demolition of part of the house would secure the safety of the remainder, it is permissible for him, indeed it is prescribed for him, in order to protect another's property. Likewise, if an oppressor wishes to seize another's property, and a person hands over part of the property as a ransom for the rest, that is permissible, even without permission.

Among its lessons: work is permissible at sea just as it is permissible on land, since He said: ﴿who work in the sea﴾, and He did not object to their work.

Among its lessons: a poor person may possess property that does not meet his needs, and this does not remove him from the designation of poverty, since God informed us that these poor people had a boat.

Among its lessons: killing is among the greatest sins, since He said regarding the killing of the boy: ﴿You have certainly done a terrible thing﴾.

Among its lessons: killing as retribution (qisas) is not objectionable, since He said: ﴿without a soul [having been killed]﴾.

Among its lessons: God protects the righteous servant in himself and in his offspring.

Among its lessons: serving the righteous, or those connected to them, is better than other things, since He ascribed the extraction of their treasure and the erection of their wall to the fact that their father was righteous.

Among its lessons: the use of good manners with God in speech. Al-Khidr attributed the defect of the boat to himself, saying: ﴿I wanted to damage it﴾, but he attributed the good to God, saying: ﴿So your Lord intended that they should reach their maturity and extract their treasure, as a mercy from your Lord﴾. Likewise Abraham (peace be upon him) said: ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾, and the jinn said: ﴿And we do not know whether evil is intended for those on earth, or whether their Lord intends for them right guidance﴾; all of this is by God's decree and divine predestination (qadar).

Among its lessons: a companion should not part from his companion in any circumstance and abandon his company until he has pleased him and made him accept his excuse, as al-Khidr did with Moses.

Among its lessons: agreeing with one's companion in matters other than those that are forbidden is a cause and means for the continuation and strengthening of companionship, just as disagreement is a cause of severing fellowship.

[Among its lessons: these events that al-Khidr carried out were a pure divine decree. God brought them about and made them occur at the hand of this righteous servant, so that the servants might infer from them His subtle kindness in His decrees, and that He may decree for the servant things he greatly dislikes, which are for the good of his religion, as in the case of the boy, or for the good of his worldly life, as in the case of the boat. Thus He showed them a model of His kindness and generosity so that they might know Him, and be utterly content with His decrees, however disagreeable.]

{60} God, exalted be He, informs about His Prophet Musa (peace be upon him) and his intense desire for good and for seeking knowledge: he said to his young servant (fata), that is, his attendant who accompanied him in residence and in travel, who was Yusha' ibn Nun, whom God later made a prophet: ﴿I will not give up until I reach the meeting place of the two seas﴾. That is: I will not cease to travel, even if the distance is long and hardship overtakes me, until I arrive at the meeting place of the two seas, which is the place where it had been revealed to him that you would find there a servant of the servants of God, the Lord of the worlds, who has knowledge that you do not have. ﴿Or I will journey on for years﴾; that is, a long distance. The meaning is that longing and desire moved Musa to make this statement to his servant.

{61} This is a firm and resolute determination from him, and therefore God carried it out. ﴿When they reached the meeting place between them, they forgot their fish﴾: they had with them a fish from which they took provision and ate, and it had been promised to him that when the fish was lost, the servant he sought would be there. ﴿And it took its way into the sea, making a tunnel﴾; that is, the fish took its path, its way, into the sea as a tunnel. This is one of the signs. The exegetes said: when that fish, from which they had been taking provision, reached that place, the water of the sea touched it, and it slipped into the sea by God's permission and joined its fellow creatures, alive.

{62} When Musa and his servant had passed the meeting place of the two seas, Musa said to his servant: ﴿Bring us our morning meal; indeed we have suffered weariness from this journey of ours﴾; that is, we have become tired from this journey beyond the meeting place, only. As for the long journey by which they reached the meeting place of the two seas, they did not feel weariness in it. This is one of the signs and indications for Musa of the presence of what he sought. Moreover, the longing connected to reaching that place made the path easy for them. So when they passed their goal, they felt the touch of weariness.

{63} When Musa said this statement to his servant, the servant said to him: ﴿Did you see when we took refuge at the rock? Indeed I forgot the fish﴾ [that is: did you not know that when night overtook us at that known rock between them, I forgot the fish]. ﴿And none caused me to forget it except Satan﴾, because he was the cause of that. ﴿And it took its way into the sea in an amazing manner﴾; that is, when it slipped into the sea and entered it, that was among the wonders. The exegetes said: that path of the fish was a tunnel, and for Musa and his servant it was a marvel.

{64} When the young man said this to him, and Musa had a promise from God that when the fish was lost he would find al-Khidr, Musa said: ﴿That is what we were seeking﴾; that is, what we were looking for. ﴿So they went back, retracing their steps﴾; that is, they returned tracing their own footprints [back] to the place where they had forgotten the fish.

{65} When they arrived there, ﴿they found a servant of Our servants﴾: he was al-Khidr, and he was a righteous servant, not a prophet according to the correct view. ﴿Whom We had given mercy from Us﴾; that is, God gave him a special mercy, by which his knowledge and good deeds increased. ﴿And taught him knowledge from Our presence﴾; that is, from Us. He had been given knowledge that Musa had not been given, although Musa (peace be upon him) was more knowledgeable than him in most matters, especially in the sciences of faith and the principles of religion, because he was one of the ulu al-'azm (the steadfast resolute messengers), whom God preferred over the rest of creation in knowledge, action and other things.

{66} When Musa met him, he said to him, out of courtesy, consultation and informing about his purpose: ﴿May I follow you on condition that you teach me of what you have been taught, as guidance?﴾; that is, may I follow you on condition that you teach me from what God has taught you, by which I may seek guidance and be guided, and by which I may know the truth in those matters. Al-Khidr had been given by God inspiration and a favor by which he came to know the inner aspects of many things that were hidden even from Musa (peace be upon him).

{67} Al-Khidr said to Musa: I do not refuse that, but ﴿you will not be able to have patience with me﴾; that is, you cannot follow me and remain with me, because you will see matters whose outward appearance is objectionable and whose inner reality is other than that, and you will not be able to bear them patiently.

{68} For this reason he said: ﴿And how can you have patience about that which you do not encompass in knowledge?﴾; that is, how can you be patient with a matter whose inner and outer aspects you have not encompassed, and whose purpose and outcome you do not know?

{69} Musa said: ﴿You will find me, God willing, patient, and I will not disobey you in any matter﴾. This was a resolution from him before the thing by which he would be tested had occurred. Resolve is one thing and the existence of patience is another; therefore Musa (peace be upon him) did not remain patient when the matter occurred.

{70} Then al-Khidr said to him: ﴿If you follow me, then do not ask me about anything until I myself mention it to you﴾; that is, do not begin with a question or objection from you until I am the one who informs you of its state at the time when it is appropriate to inform you. So he forbade him from questioning him, and promised that he would make him understand the reality of the matter.

{71} ﴿So they went on until, when they boarded the boat, he made a hole in it﴾; that is, al-Khidr pulled a plank from it, and he had an aim in that which he would later explain. Musa (peace be upon him) did not remain patient, because its outward appearance was objectionable: it was a defect in the boat and a cause of the drowning of its people. Therefore Musa said: ﴿Have you made a hole in it to drown its people? You have certainly done a terrible thing﴾; that is, something great and monstrous. This was from his lack of patience (peace be upon him).

{72} Al-Khidr said to him: ﴿Did I not say that you would not be able to have patience with me?﴾; that is, it happened as I had told you.

{73} This was from Musa out of forgetfulness. He said: ﴿Do not take me to task for what I forgot, and do not burden me with difficulty in my affair﴾; that is, do not make the matter difficult for me, and be lenient with me, for that occurred through forgetfulness. So do not hold me accountable the first time. He combined acknowledgment of it with an excuse for it, and that it was not proper for you, O Khidr, to be harsh with your companion. So al-Khidr forgave him.

{74} ﴿So they went on until, when they met a boy﴾; that is, a young boy. ﴿So he killed him﴾: al-Khidr. Musa was seized with great anger, and religious zeal overcame him when he killed a young boy who had committed no sin. ﴿He said: Have you killed an innocent soul without its having killed anyone? You have certainly done a dreadful thing﴾. What could be more dreadful than killing a young child who had no sin and had killed no one? The first lapse from Musa was forgetfulness, but this was not forgetfulness; it was a lack of patience.

{75} Al-Khidr said to him, admonishing and reminding him: ﴿Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?﴾

{76} So Musa said to him: ﴿If I ask you about anything after this, then do not keep me as a companion﴾; that is, you are excused in that and in ending my companionship. ﴿You have indeed received an excuse from me﴾; that is, you have made me give an excuse, and you did not fall short.

{77} ﴿So they went on until, when they came to the people of a town, they asked its people for food﴾; that is, they asked them for hospitality, but they did not host them. ﴿And they found in it a wall about to collapse﴾; that is, [it had] become defective and ruined. ﴿So he set it upright﴾: al-Khidr; that is, he built it and restored it as new. Musa said to him: ﴿If you had wished, you could have taken payment for it﴾; that is, the people of this town did not host us even though it was obligatory for them, and you build it without wages, though you are capable of taking them?

{78} At that point Musa (peace be upon him) did not keep what he had said, and al-Khidr made him an excuse. So he said to him: ﴿This is the parting between me and you﴾: for you had stipulated that condition upon yourself, so now there is no excuse and no place for companionship. ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of that about which you could not have patience﴾; that is, I will tell you what you objected to in me, and inform you that for me in it there were purposes and what the matter would lead to.

{79} ﴿As for the boat, it belonged to poor people who worked on the sea﴾: which requires compassion toward them and kindness to them. ﴿So I wanted to damage it, for behind them was a king who seized every boat by force﴾; that is, their passage was past that unjust king. Every sound boat that passed him without defect, he would seize and take unjustly. So I wanted to make a hole in it, so that it would have a defect and be safe from that oppressor.

{80} ﴿As for the boy, his parents were believers, and we feared that he would burden them with rebellion and disbelief﴾: and that boy had been decreed to be such that if he reached maturity, he would burden his parents with rebellion and disbelief; that is, he would force them into rebellion and disbelief, either out of their love for him or because of their need for him, or he would drive them to that. So I killed him, because I knew of that, to preserve the religion of his two believing parents. What benefit could be greater than this noble benefit?

{81} Although it involved harm to them and cutting off their offspring, God, exalted be He, would give them offspring better than him. For this reason He said: ﴿So We wanted their Lord to replace him for them with one better in purity and nearer in kinship﴾; that is, a righteous son, pure, and keeping ties of kinship. For the boy who was killed, if he had reached maturity, would have disobeyed his parents in the most severe way by forcing them into disbelief and rebellion.

{82} As for the wall: that which I set upright, ﴿it belonged to two orphan boys in the town, and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them, and their father had been righteous﴾; that is, their situation called for compassion and mercy toward them, because they were young and had lost their father, and God also preserved them through the righteousness of their father. ﴿So your Lord willed that they reach maturity and extract their treasure﴾; that is, for this reason I tore down the wall, extracted what was beneath it of their treasure, returned it to them, and rebuilt it without payment. ﴿As a mercy from your Lord﴾; that is, what I did was a mercy from God, which God gave to His servant al-Khidr. ﴿And I did not do it of my own accord﴾; that is, I did not do anything on my own initiative or by my own mere will, but it was from God's mercy and His command. ﴿That is the interpretation of that about which you could not have patience﴾: which I have explained to you.

In this wondrous and noble story there are many benefits, rulings and principles, and we will point out some of them, with God's help:

Among them: the virtue of knowledge and of journeying in its pursuit, and that it is among the most important matters. Musa (peace be upon him) traveled a long distance, suffered weariness in seeking it, and left off sitting with the Children of Israel to teach and guide them, choosing travel to increase his knowledge over that.

Among them: beginning with the more important and then the more important: increasing knowledge and a person's own knowledge is more important than abandoning that and occupying oneself with teaching without having provided oneself with knowledge; combining both is more complete.

Among them: the permissibility of taking a servant both at home and while traveling, to meet needs and seek comfort, as Musa did.

Among them: that the traveler seeking knowledge, or jihad, or something similar, if the benefit requires informing others of his purpose and where he intends to go, then this is more complete than concealing it; for in making it known there are benefits: preparing its provisions, undertaking the matter with insight, and showing longing for this noble act of worship, as Musa said: ﴿I will not give up until I reach the meeting place of the two seas, or I will journey on for years﴾; and as the Prophet (ﷺ) informed his companions when he marched to Tabuk, stating his direction openly, although his habit was to use indirect speech; and that was in accordance with what benefits.

Among them: attributing evil and its causes to Satan, in the sense of enticement and adornment, although everything is by God's decree and determination, as in the statement of Musa's servant: ﴿And none caused me to forget it except Satan, that I should mention it﴾.

Among them: the permissibility of a person reporting what is part of the nature of the soul, such as weariness, hunger or thirst, when it is not in the manner of complaining bitterly and is truthful; as in Musa's statement: ﴿We have indeed suffered weariness from this journey of ours﴾.

Among them: the recommendation that a person's servant be clever, perceptive and shrewd, so that the matter he intends may be accomplished for him.

Among them: the recommendation that a person feed his servant from his own food, and that they eat together; for the apparent meaning of his words ﴿Bring us our morning meal﴾, attributing it to all of them, is that he and his servant both ate.

Among them: that help descends upon the servant according to his fulfilling what he is commanded, and that one who complies with God's command is helped in ways that others are not helped; as in His statement ﴿We have indeed suffered weariness from this journey of ours﴾, referring to the journey beyond the meeting place of the two seas. As for the first journey, they did not complain of weariness during it despite its length, because it was the true journey. As for the last one, it apparently lasted part of a day, because they lost the fish when they took refuge at the rock; so apparently they spent the night there, then they set out the next day, until when it came time for the morning meal, Musa said to his servant: ﴿Bring us our morning meal﴾; then he remembered that he had forgotten it at the place which was the end of his goal.

Among them: that this servant whom they met was not a prophet, but a righteous servant; for He described him with servanthood, and mentioned God's favor upon him with mercy and knowledge, and did not mention his messengership or prophethood; and had he been a prophet, that would have been mentioned as it was mentioned for others. As for his statement at the end of the story: ﴿And I did not do it of my own accord﴾, it does not indicate that he was a prophet, but indicates inspiration and being spoken to by God, as is the case for non-prophets, as God, exalted be He, said: ﴿And We inspired the mother of Musa: suckle him﴾, and ﴿Your Lord inspired the bee: take for yourself houses in the mountains﴾.

Among them: that knowledge which God teaches His servants is of two kinds: acquired knowledge, which the servant attains through his diligence and effort; and a kind of knowledge given directly from God (ladunni), which God bestows on whom He favors among His servants; as in His statement: ﴿And We taught him knowledge from Our presence﴾.

Among them: courtesy toward the teacher, and that the student addresses him in the gentlest manner; as in the words of Musa (peace be upon him): ﴿May I follow you on condition that you teach me of what you have been taught, as guidance?﴾. He phrased his speech in a manner of gentleness and consultation: whether you permit me in that or not. And his acknowledgment that he is learning from him, unlike the case of those who are rude or proud, who do not show the teacher their need for his knowledge, but claim that they cooperate with him, and may even think that they are teaching their teacher while being utterly ignorant. Humbling oneself before the teacher and showing one's need to be taught is among the most beneficial things for the student.

Among them: the humility of the superior person in learning from one who is below him; for Musa was without doubt superior to al-Khidr.

Among them: the learning of a superior scholar in a field in which he has not mastered from one who has mastered it, even if the latter is below him in knowledge by many degrees; for Musa (peace be upon him) was among the ulu al-'azm (steadfast resolute messengers), whom God granted and gave knowledge that He gave to no one else; but in this specific knowledge, al-Khidr had what Musa did not have. Therefore he eagerly sought to learn from him. On this basis, it is not appropriate for a jurist or hadith scholar who is deficient in the science of grammar (nahw), morphology (sarf), or similar disciplines to refrain from learning them from one who has mastered them, even if he himself is not a hadith scholar or jurist.

Among them: attributing knowledge and other virtues to God, the Exalted, acknowledging that, and thanking God for them; as in His statement ﴿that you teach me of what you have been taught﴾; that is, of what God, the Exalted, has taught you.

Among them: that beneficial knowledge is knowledge that guides to good. Every knowledge that contains guidance and direction to the path of good, and warning against the path of evil or a means to that, is beneficial knowledge. Anything beyond that is either harmful or has no benefit; as in His statement ﴿that you teach me of what you have been taught, as guidance﴾.

Among them: that whoever lacks the strength of patience in keeping company with a scholar and with knowledge, and lacks steadfastness in that, will lose much of the knowledge in proportion to his lack of patience. Whoever lacks patience does not attain knowledge, and whoever employs patience and persists in it attains through it every matter he strives for. This is shown by al-Khidr's statement, excusing himself to Musa by mentioning the obstacle that prevents Musa from learning from him: that he would not be able to remain patient with him.

Among them: that a major cause of attaining patience is a person's comprehensive knowledge and experience of the matter for which he has been commanded to be patient; otherwise, one who does not understand it, or does not understand its end, result, benefit or fruit, does not possess the cause of patience. This is shown by His statement ﴿And how can you have patience about that which you do not encompass in knowledge?﴾; so He made the reason for his lack of patience his failure to comprehend the matter in knowledge.

Among them: the command to be deliberate and careful, and not to rush to judge a thing until one knows what is intended by it and what its purpose is.

Among them: making future actions that depend on human choice conditional upon God's will, and that a person should not say of something: "I will do that in the future," except by saying "God willing."

Among them: that resolving to do something is not the same as doing it; for Musa said: ﴿You will find me, God willing, patient﴾.

Then he resolved to be patient, but he did not do so.

Among its lessons: when the teacher sees that it is in the student's interest to be restrained from beginning to ask about certain matters, so that the teacher is the one who brings him to them, then the teacher may do so, since benefit follows what is best. This applies, for example, when the student's understanding is limited, or when the teacher forbids him from probing into matters whose importance is less than others, or matters his mind cannot grasp, or when he asks a question that is not relevant to the subject under discussion.

Among its lessons: it is permissible to board the sea in circumstances other than those in which one fears for one's safety.

Among its lessons: the one who forgets is not held accountable for his forgetting, neither in respect of the rights of God nor in respect of the rights of people, since He said: ﴿Do not hold me accountable for what I forgot﴾.

Among its lessons: a person should take from people's characters and dealings what is easy and what they willingly give, and he should not burden them with what they cannot bear or what would be hard and oppressive for them, for this leads to aversion and weariness. Rather, he should take what is readily available, so that the matter becomes easy for him.

Among its lessons: matters are judged by their outward appearance, and worldly rulings concerning property, blood and other things depend upon it. Moses (peace be upon him) objected to al-Khidr's damaging of the boat and killing of the boy, and these matters outwardly appear to be wrongful. Moses (peace be upon him) could not remain silent about them in circumstances other than those in which he accompanied al-Khidr. So he was hasty, rushed to judgment according to their general state, and did not heed this incidental factor which obliged him to be patient and not to hasten to object.

Among its lessons: the great and sublime principle (qa'idah) that a greater evil is averted by committing a lesser evil, and the greater of two benefits is preserved by forgoing the lesser of them. The killing of the boy was an evil, but his remaining alive until he tempted his parents away from their religion was a greater evil than that, and his remaining alive without being killed and preserved, even if one supposes it to be good, is less good than preserving his parents' religion and their faith. Therefore al-Khidr killed him. Under this principle there are branches and benefits that cannot be enumerated, and the clashing of all benefits and harms falls under it.

Among its lessons: another great principle, namely that a person's action concerning another's property, when done for the sake of benefit and removing harm, is permissible, even without permission, and even if his action results in the destruction of part of another's property. Just as al-Khidr damaged the boat so that it would be defective and thus be safe from the seizure of the oppressive king. Accordingly: if a fire, a flood or something similar occurs in a person's house or property, and the destruction of some of the property or the demolition of part of the house would secure the safety of the remainder, it is permissible for him, indeed it is prescribed for him, in order to protect another's property. Likewise, if an oppressor wishes to seize another's property, and a person hands over part of the property as a ransom for the rest, that is permissible, even without permission.

Among its lessons: work is permissible at sea just as it is permissible on land, since He said: ﴿who work in the sea﴾, and He did not object to their work.

Among its lessons: a poor person may possess property that does not meet his needs, and this does not remove him from the designation of poverty, since God informed us that these poor people had a boat.

Among its lessons: killing is among the greatest sins, since He said regarding the killing of the boy: ﴿You have certainly done a terrible thing﴾.

Among its lessons: killing as retribution (qisas) is not objectionable, since He said: ﴿without a soul [having been killed]﴾.

Among its lessons: God protects the righteous servant in himself and in his offspring.

Among its lessons: serving the righteous, or those connected to them, is better than other things, since He ascribed the extraction of their treasure and the erection of their wall to the fact that their father was righteous.

Among its lessons: the use of good manners with God in speech. Al-Khidr attributed the defect of the boat to himself, saying: ﴿I wanted to damage it﴾, but he attributed the good to God, saying: ﴿So your Lord intended that they should reach their maturity and extract their treasure, as a mercy from your Lord﴾. Likewise Abraham (peace be upon him) said: ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾, and the jinn said: ﴿And we do not know whether evil is intended for those on earth, or whether their Lord intends for them right guidance﴾; all of this is by God's decree and divine predestination (qadar).

Among its lessons: a companion should not part from his companion in any circumstance and abandon his company until he has pleased him and made him accept his excuse, as al-Khidr did with Moses.

Among its lessons: agreeing with one's companion in matters other than those that are forbidden is a cause and means for the continuation and strengthening of companionship, just as disagreement is a cause of severing fellowship.

[Among its lessons: these events that al-Khidr carried out were a pure divine decree. God brought them about and made them occur at the hand of this righteous servant, so that the servants might infer from them His subtle kindness in His decrees, and that He may decree for the servant things he greatly dislikes, which are for the good of his religion, as in the case of the boy, or for the good of his worldly life, as in the case of the boat. Thus He showed them a model of His kindness and generosity so that they might know Him, and be utterly content with His decrees, however disagreeable.]

{60} God, exalted be He, informs about His Prophet Musa (peace be upon him) and his intense desire for good and for seeking knowledge: he said to his young servant (fata), that is, his attendant who accompanied him in residence and in travel, who was Yusha' ibn Nun, whom God later made a prophet: ﴿I will not give up until I reach the meeting place of the two seas﴾. That is: I will not cease to travel, even if the distance is long and hardship overtakes me, until I arrive at the meeting place of the two seas, which is the place where it had been revealed to him that you would find there a servant of the servants of God, the Lord of the worlds, who has knowledge that you do not have. ﴿Or I will journey on for years﴾; that is, a long distance. The meaning is that longing and desire moved Musa to make this statement to his servant.

{61} This is a firm and resolute determination from him, and therefore God carried it out. ﴿When they reached the meeting place between them, they forgot their fish﴾: they had with them a fish from which they took provision and ate, and it had been promised to him that when the fish was lost, the servant he sought would be there. ﴿And it took its way into the sea, making a tunnel﴾; that is, the fish took its path, its way, into the sea as a tunnel. This is one of the signs. The exegetes said: when that fish, from which they had been taking provision, reached that place, the water of the sea touched it, and it slipped into the sea by God's permission and joined its fellow creatures, alive.

{62} When Musa and his servant had passed the meeting place of the two seas, Musa said to his servant: ﴿Bring us our morning meal; indeed we have suffered weariness from this journey of ours﴾; that is, we have become tired from this journey beyond the meeting place, only. As for the long journey by which they reached the meeting place of the two seas, they did not feel weariness in it. This is one of the signs and indications for Musa of the presence of what he sought. Moreover, the longing connected to reaching that place made the path easy for them. So when they passed their goal, they felt the touch of weariness.

{63} When Musa said this statement to his servant, the servant said to him: ﴿Did you see when we took refuge at the rock? Indeed I forgot the fish﴾ [that is: did you not know that when night overtook us at that known rock between them, I forgot the fish]. ﴿And none caused me to forget it except Satan﴾, because he was the cause of that. ﴿And it took its way into the sea in an amazing manner﴾; that is, when it slipped into the sea and entered it, that was among the wonders. The exegetes said: that path of the fish was a tunnel, and for Musa and his servant it was a marvel.

{64} When the young man said this to him, and Musa had a promise from God that when the fish was lost he would find al-Khidr, Musa said: ﴿That is what we were seeking﴾; that is, what we were looking for. ﴿So they went back, retracing their steps﴾; that is, they returned tracing their own footprints [back] to the place where they had forgotten the fish.

{65} When they arrived there, ﴿they found a servant of Our servants﴾: he was al-Khidr, and he was a righteous servant, not a prophet according to the correct view. ﴿Whom We had given mercy from Us﴾; that is, God gave him a special mercy, by which his knowledge and good deeds increased. ﴿And taught him knowledge from Our presence﴾; that is, from Us. He had been given knowledge that Musa had not been given, although Musa (peace be upon him) was more knowledgeable than him in most matters, especially in the sciences of faith and the principles of religion, because he was one of the ulu al-'azm (the steadfast resolute messengers), whom God preferred over the rest of creation in knowledge, action and other things.

{66} When Musa met him, he said to him, out of courtesy, consultation and informing about his purpose: ﴿May I follow you on condition that you teach me of what you have been taught, as guidance?﴾; that is, may I follow you on condition that you teach me from what God has taught you, by which I may seek guidance and be guided, and by which I may know the truth in those matters. Al-Khidr had been given by God inspiration and a favor by which he came to know the inner aspects of many things that were hidden even from Musa (peace be upon him).

{67} Al-Khidr said to Musa: I do not refuse that, but ﴿you will not be able to have patience with me﴾; that is, you cannot follow me and remain with me, because you will see matters whose outward appearance is objectionable and whose inner reality is other than that, and you will not be able to bear them patiently.

{68} For this reason he said: ﴿And how can you have patience about that which you do not encompass in knowledge?﴾; that is, how can you be patient with a matter whose inner and outer aspects you have not encompassed, and whose purpose and outcome you do not know?

{69} Musa said: ﴿You will find me, God willing, patient, and I will not disobey you in any matter﴾. This was a resolution from him before the thing by which he would be tested had occurred. Resolve is one thing and the existence of patience is another; therefore Musa (peace be upon him) did not remain patient when the matter occurred.

{70} Then al-Khidr said to him: ﴿If you follow me, then do not ask me about anything until I myself mention it to you﴾; that is, do not begin with a question or objection from you until I am the one who informs you of its state at the time when it is appropriate to inform you. So he forbade him from questioning him, and promised that he would make him understand the reality of the matter.

{71} ﴿So they went on until, when they boarded the boat, he made a hole in it﴾; that is, al-Khidr pulled a plank from it, and he had an aim in that which he would later explain. Musa (peace be upon him) did not remain patient, because its outward appearance was objectionable: it was a defect in the boat and a cause of the drowning of its people. Therefore Musa said: ﴿Have you made a hole in it to drown its people? You have certainly done a terrible thing﴾; that is, something great and monstrous. This was from his lack of patience (peace be upon him).

{72} Al-Khidr said to him: ﴿Did I not say that you would not be able to have patience with me?﴾; that is, it happened as I had told you.

{73} This was from Musa out of forgetfulness. He said: ﴿Do not take me to task for what I forgot, and do not burden me with difficulty in my affair﴾; that is, do not make the matter difficult for me, and be lenient with me, for that occurred through forgetfulness. So do not hold me accountable the first time. He combined acknowledgment of it with an excuse for it, and that it was not proper for you, O Khidr, to be harsh with your companion. So al-Khidr forgave him.

{74} ﴿So they went on until, when they met a boy﴾; that is, a young boy. ﴿So he killed him﴾: al-Khidr. Musa was seized with great anger, and religious zeal overcame him when he killed a young boy who had committed no sin. ﴿He said: Have you killed an innocent soul without its having killed anyone? You have certainly done a dreadful thing﴾. What could be more dreadful than killing a young child who had no sin and had killed no one? The first lapse from Musa was forgetfulness, but this was not forgetfulness; it was a lack of patience.

{75} Al-Khidr said to him, admonishing and reminding him: ﴿Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?﴾

{76} So Musa said to him: ﴿If I ask you about anything after this, then do not keep me as a companion﴾; that is, you are excused in that and in ending my companionship. ﴿You have indeed received an excuse from me﴾; that is, you have made me give an excuse, and you did not fall short.

{77} ﴿So they went on until, when they came to the people of a town, they asked its people for food﴾; that is, they asked them for hospitality, but they did not host them. ﴿And they found in it a wall about to collapse﴾; that is, [it had] become defective and ruined. ﴿So he set it upright﴾: al-Khidr; that is, he built it and restored it as new. Musa said to him: ﴿If you had wished, you could have taken payment for it﴾; that is, the people of this town did not host us even though it was obligatory for them, and you build it without wages, though you are capable of taking them?

{78} At that point Musa (peace be upon him) did not keep what he had said, and al-Khidr made him an excuse. So he said to him: ﴿This is the parting between me and you﴾: for you had stipulated that condition upon yourself, so now there is no excuse and no place for companionship. ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of that about which you could not have patience﴾; that is, I will tell you what you objected to in me, and inform you that for me in it there were purposes and what the matter would lead to.

{79} ﴿As for the boat, it belonged to poor people who worked on the sea﴾: which requires compassion toward them and kindness to them. ﴿So I wanted to damage it, for behind them was a king who seized every boat by force﴾; that is, their passage was past that unjust king. Every sound boat that passed him without defect, he would seize and take unjustly. So I wanted to make a hole in it, so that it would have a defect and be safe from that oppressor.

{80} ﴿As for the boy, his parents were believers, and we feared that he would burden them with rebellion and disbelief﴾: and that boy had been decreed to be such that if he reached maturity, he would burden his parents with rebellion and disbelief; that is, he would force them into rebellion and disbelief, either out of their love for him or because of their need for him, or he would drive them to that. So I killed him, because I knew of that, to preserve the religion of his two believing parents. What benefit could be greater than this noble benefit?

{81} Although it involved harm to them and cutting off their offspring, God, exalted be He, would give them offspring better than him. For this reason He said: ﴿So We wanted their Lord to replace him for them with one better in purity and nearer in kinship﴾; that is, a righteous son, pure, and keeping ties of kinship. For the boy who was killed, if he had reached maturity, would have disobeyed his parents in the most severe way by forcing them into disbelief and rebellion.

{82} As for the wall: that which I set upright, ﴿it belonged to two orphan boys in the town, and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them, and their father had been righteous﴾; that is, their situation called for compassion and mercy toward them, because they were young and had lost their father, and God also preserved them through the righteousness of their father. ﴿So your Lord willed that they reach maturity and extract their treasure﴾; that is, for this reason I tore down the wall, extracted what was beneath it of their treasure, returned it to them, and rebuilt it without payment. ﴿As a mercy from your Lord﴾; that is, what I did was a mercy from God, which God gave to His servant al-Khidr. ﴿And I did not do it of my own accord﴾; that is, I did not do anything on my own initiative or by my own mere will, but it was from God's mercy and His command. ﴿That is the interpretation of that about which you could not have patience﴾: which I have explained to you.

Among them: that resolving to do something is not the same as doing it; for Musa said: ﴿You will find me, God willing, patient﴾.

Then he resolved to be patient, but he did not do so.

Among its lessons: when the teacher sees that it is in the student's interest to be restrained from beginning to ask about certain matters, so that the teacher is the one who brings him to them, then the teacher may do so, since benefit follows what is best. This applies, for example, when the student's understanding is limited, or when the teacher forbids him from probing into matters whose importance is less than others, or matters his mind cannot grasp, or when he asks a question that is not relevant to the subject under discussion.

Among its lessons: it is permissible to board the sea in circumstances other than those in which one fears for one's safety.

Among its lessons: the one who forgets is not held accountable for his forgetting, neither in respect of the rights of God nor in respect of the rights of people, since He said: ﴿Do not hold me accountable for what I forgot﴾.

Among its lessons: a person should take from people's characters and dealings what is easy and what they willingly give, and he should not burden them with what they cannot bear or what would be hard and oppressive for them, for this leads to aversion and weariness. Rather, he should take what is readily available, so that the matter becomes easy for him.

Among its lessons: matters are judged by their outward appearance, and worldly rulings concerning property, blood and other things depend upon it. Moses (peace be upon him) objected to al-Khidr's damaging of the boat and killing of the boy, and these matters outwardly appear to be wrongful. Moses (peace be upon him) could not remain silent about them in circumstances other than those in which he accompanied al-Khidr. So he was hasty, rushed to judgment according to their general state, and did not heed this incidental factor which obliged him to be patient and not to hasten to object.

Among its lessons: the great and sublime principle (qa'idah) that a greater evil is averted by committing a lesser evil, and the greater of two benefits is preserved by forgoing the lesser of them. The killing of the boy was an evil, but his remaining alive until he tempted his parents away from their religion was a greater evil than that, and his remaining alive without being killed and preserved, even if one supposes it to be good, is less good than preserving his parents' religion and their faith. Therefore al-Khidr killed him. Under this principle there are branches and benefits that cannot be enumerated, and the clashing of all benefits and harms falls under it.

Among its lessons: another great principle, namely that a person's action concerning another's property, when done for the sake of benefit and removing harm, is permissible, even without permission, and even if his action results in the destruction of part of another's property. Just as al-Khidr damaged the boat so that it would be defective and thus be safe from the seizure of the oppressive king. Accordingly: if a fire, a flood or something similar occurs in a person's house or property, and the destruction of some of the property or the demolition of part of the house would secure the safety of the remainder, it is permissible for him, indeed it is prescribed for him, in order to protect another's property. Likewise, if an oppressor wishes to seize another's property, and a person hands over part of the property as a ransom for the rest, that is permissible, even without permission.

Among its lessons: work is permissible at sea just as it is permissible on land, since He said: ﴿who work in the sea﴾, and He did not object to their work.

Among its lessons: a poor person may possess property that does not meet his needs, and this does not remove him from the designation of poverty, since God informed us that these poor people had a boat.

Among its lessons: killing is among the greatest sins, since He said regarding the killing of the boy: ﴿You have certainly done a terrible thing﴾.

Among its lessons: killing as retribution (qisas) is not objectionable, since He said: ﴿without a soul [having been killed]﴾.

Among its lessons: God protects the righteous servant in himself and in his offspring.

Among its lessons: serving the righteous, or those connected to them, is better than other things, since He ascribed the extraction of their treasure and the erection of their wall to the fact that their father was righteous.

Among its lessons: the use of good manners with God in speech. Al-Khidr attributed the defect of the boat to himself, saying: ﴿I wanted to damage it﴾, but he attributed the good to God, saying: ﴿So your Lord intended that they should reach their maturity and extract their treasure, as a mercy from your Lord﴾. Likewise Abraham (peace be upon him) said: ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾, and the jinn said: ﴿And we do not know whether evil is intended for those on earth, or whether their Lord intends for them right guidance﴾; all of this is by God's decree and divine predestination (qadar).

Among its lessons: a companion should not part from his companion in any circumstance and abandon his company until he has pleased him and made him accept his excuse, as al-Khidr did with Moses.

Among its lessons: agreeing with one's companion in matters other than those that are forbidden is a cause and means for the continuation and strengthening of companionship, just as disagreement is a cause of severing fellowship.

[Among its lessons: these events that al-Khidr carried out were a pure divine decree. God brought them about and made them occur at the hand of this righteous servant, so that the servants might infer from them His subtle kindness in His decrees, and that He may decree for the servant things he greatly dislikes, which are for the good of his religion, as in the case of the boy, or for the good of his worldly life, as in the case of the boat. Thus He showed them a model of His kindness and generosity so that they might know Him, and be utterly content with His decrees, however disagreeable.]

{60} God, exalted be He, informs about His Prophet Musa (peace be upon him) and his intense desire for good and for seeking knowledge: he said to his young servant (fata), that is, his attendant who accompanied him in residence and in travel, who was Yusha' ibn Nun, whom God later made a prophet: ﴿I will not give up until I reach the meeting place of the two seas﴾. That is: I will not cease to travel, even if the distance is long and hardship overtakes me, until I arrive at the meeting place of the two seas, which is the place where it had been revealed to him that you would find there a servant of the servants of God, the Lord of the worlds, who has knowledge that you do not have. ﴿Or I will journey on for years﴾; that is, a long distance. The meaning is that longing and desire moved Musa to make this statement to his servant.

{61} This is a firm and resolute determination from him, and therefore God carried it out. ﴿When they reached the meeting place between them, they forgot their fish﴾: they had with them a fish from which they took provision and ate, and it had been promised to him that when the fish was lost, the servant he sought would be there. ﴿And it took its way into the sea, making a tunnel﴾; that is, the fish took its path, its way, into the sea as a tunnel. This is one of the signs. The exegetes said: when that fish, from which they had been taking provision, reached that place, the water of the sea touched it, and it slipped into the sea by God's permission and joined its fellow creatures, alive.

{62} When Musa and his servant had passed the meeting place of the two seas, Musa said to his servant: ﴿Bring us our morning meal; indeed we have suffered weariness from this journey of ours﴾; that is, we have become tired from this journey beyond the meeting place, only. As for the long journey by which they reached the meeting place of the two seas, they did not feel weariness in it. This is one of the signs and indications for Musa of the presence of what he sought. Moreover, the longing connected to reaching that place made the path easy for them. So when they passed their goal, they felt the touch of weariness.

{63} When Musa said this statement to his servant, the servant said to him: ﴿Did you see when we took refuge at the rock? Indeed I forgot the fish﴾ [that is: did you not know that when night overtook us at that known rock between them, I forgot the fish]. ﴿And none caused me to forget it except Satan﴾, because he was the cause of that. ﴿And it took its way into the sea in an amazing manner﴾; that is, when it slipped into the sea and entered it, that was among the wonders. The exegetes said: that path of the fish was a tunnel, and for Musa and his servant it was a marvel.

{64} When the young man said this to him, and Musa had a promise from God that when the fish was lost he would find al-Khidr, Musa said: ﴿That is what we were seeking﴾; that is, what we were looking for. ﴿So they went back, retracing their steps﴾; that is, they returned tracing their own footprints [back] to the place where they had forgotten the fish.

{65} When they arrived there, ﴿they found a servant of Our servants﴾: he was al-Khidr, and he was a righteous servant, not a prophet according to the correct view. ﴿Whom We had given mercy from Us﴾; that is, God gave him a special mercy, by which his knowledge and good deeds increased. ﴿And taught him knowledge from Our presence﴾; that is, from Us. He had been given knowledge that Musa had not been given, although Musa (peace be upon him) was more knowledgeable than him in most matters, especially in the sciences of faith and the principles of religion, because he was one of the ulu al-'azm (the steadfast resolute messengers), whom God preferred over the rest of creation in knowledge, action and other things.

{66} When Musa met him, he said to him, out of courtesy, consultation and informing about his purpose: ﴿May I follow you on condition that you teach me of what you have been taught, as guidance?﴾; that is, may I follow you on condition that you teach me from what God has taught you, by which I may seek guidance and be guided, and by which I may know the truth in those matters. Al-Khidr had been given by God inspiration and a favor by which he came to know the inner aspects of many things that were hidden even from Musa (peace be upon him).

{67} Al-Khidr said to Musa: I do not refuse that, but ﴿you will not be able to have patience with me﴾; that is, you cannot follow me and remain with me, because you will see matters whose outward appearance is objectionable and whose inner reality is other than that, and you will not be able to bear them patiently.

{68} For this reason he said: ﴿And how can you have patience about that which you do not encompass in knowledge?﴾; that is, how can you be patient with a matter whose inner and outer aspects you have not encompassed, and whose purpose and outcome you do not know?

{69} Musa said: ﴿You will find me, God willing, patient, and I will not disobey you in any matter﴾. This was a resolution from him before the thing by which he would be tested had occurred. Resolve is one thing and the existence of patience is another; therefore Musa (peace be upon him) did not remain patient when the matter occurred.

{70} Then al-Khidr said to him: ﴿If you follow me, then do not ask me about anything until I myself mention it to you﴾; that is, do not begin with a question or objection from you until I am the one who informs you of its state at the time when it is appropriate to inform you. So he forbade him from questioning him, and promised that he would make him understand the reality of the matter.

{71} ﴿So they went on until, when they boarded the boat, he made a hole in it﴾; that is, al-Khidr pulled a plank from it, and he had an aim in that which he would later explain. Musa (peace be upon him) did not remain patient, because its outward appearance was objectionable: it was a defect in the boat and a cause of the drowning of its people. Therefore Musa said: ﴿Have you made a hole in it to drown its people? You have certainly done a terrible thing﴾; that is, something great and monstrous. This was from his lack of patience (peace be upon him).

{72} Al-Khidr said to him: ﴿Did I not say that you would not be able to have patience with me?﴾; that is, it happened as I had told you.

{73} This was from Musa out of forgetfulness. He said: ﴿Do not take me to task for what I forgot, and do not burden me with difficulty in my affair﴾; that is, do not make the matter difficult for me, and be lenient with me, for that occurred through forgetfulness. So do not hold me accountable the first time. He combined acknowledgment of it with an excuse for it, and that it was not proper for you, O Khidr, to be harsh with your companion. So al-Khidr forgave him.

{74} ﴿So they went on until, when they met a boy﴾; that is, a young boy. ﴿So he killed him﴾: al-Khidr. Musa was seized with great anger, and religious zeal overcame him when he killed a young boy who had committed no sin. ﴿He said: Have you killed an innocent soul without its having killed anyone? You have certainly done a dreadful thing﴾. What could be more dreadful than killing a young child who had no sin and had killed no one? The first lapse from Musa was forgetfulness, but this was not forgetfulness; it was a lack of patience.

{75} Al-Khidr said to him, admonishing and reminding him: ﴿Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?﴾

{76} So Musa said to him: ﴿If I ask you about anything after this, then do not keep me as a companion﴾; that is, you are excused in that and in ending my companionship. ﴿You have indeed received an excuse from me﴾; that is, you have made me give an excuse, and you did not fall short.

{77} ﴿So they went on until, when they came to the people of a town, they asked its people for food﴾; that is, they asked them for hospitality, but they did not host them. ﴿And they found in it a wall about to collapse﴾; that is, [it had] become defective and ruined. ﴿So he set it upright﴾: al-Khidr; that is, he built it and restored it as new. Musa said to him: ﴿If you had wished, you could have taken payment for it﴾; that is, the people of this town did not host us even though it was obligatory for them, and you build it without wages, though you are capable of taking them?

{78} At that point Musa (peace be upon him) did not keep what he had said, and al-Khidr made him an excuse. So he said to him: ﴿This is the parting between me and you﴾: for you had stipulated that condition upon yourself, so now there is no excuse and no place for companionship. ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of that about which you could not have patience﴾; that is, I will tell you what you objected to in me, and inform you that for me in it there were purposes and what the matter would lead to.

{79} ﴿As for the boat, it belonged to poor people who worked on the sea﴾: which requires compassion toward them and kindness to them. ﴿So I wanted to damage it, for behind them was a king who seized every boat by force﴾; that is, their passage was past that unjust king. Every sound boat that passed him without defect, he would seize and take unjustly. So I wanted to make a hole in it, so that it would have a defect and be safe from that oppressor.

{80} ﴿As for the boy, his parents were believers, and we feared that he would burden them with rebellion and disbelief﴾: and that boy had been decreed to be such that if he reached maturity, he would burden his parents with rebellion and disbelief; that is, he would force them into rebellion and disbelief, either out of their love for him or because of their need for him, or he would drive them to that. So I killed him, because I knew of that, to preserve the religion of his two believing parents. What benefit could be greater than this noble benefit?

{81} Although it involved harm to them and cutting off their offspring, God, exalted be He, would give them offspring better than him. For this reason He said: ﴿So We wanted their Lord to replace him for them with one better in purity and nearer in kinship﴾; that is, a righteous son, pure, and keeping ties of kinship. For the boy who was killed, if he had reached maturity, would have disobeyed his parents in the most severe way by forcing them into disbelief and rebellion.

{82} As for the wall: that which I set upright, ﴿it belonged to two orphan boys in the town, and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them, and their father had been righteous﴾; that is, their situation called for compassion and mercy toward them, because they were young and had lost their father, and God also preserved them through the righteousness of their father. ﴿So your Lord willed that they reach maturity and extract their treasure﴾; that is, for this reason I tore down the wall, extracted what was beneath it of their treasure, returned it to them, and rebuilt it without payment. ﴿As a mercy from your Lord﴾; that is, what I did was a mercy from God, which God gave to His servant al-Khidr. ﴿And I did not do it of my own accord﴾; that is, I did not do anything on my own initiative or by my own mere will, but it was from God's mercy and His command. ﴿That is the interpretation of that about which you could not have patience﴾: which I have explained to you.

In this wondrous and noble story there are many benefits, rulings and principles, and we will point out some of them, with God's help:

Among them: the virtue of knowledge and of journeying in its pursuit, and that it is among the most important matters. Musa (peace be upon him) traveled a long distance, suffered weariness in seeking it, and left off sitting with the Children of Israel to teach and guide them, choosing travel to increase his knowledge over that.

Among them: beginning with the more important and then the more important: increasing knowledge and a person's own knowledge is more important than abandoning that and occupying oneself with teaching without having provided oneself with knowledge; combining both is more complete.

Among them: the permissibility of taking a servant both at home and while traveling, to meet needs and seek comfort, as Musa did.

Among them: that the traveler seeking knowledge, or jihad, or something similar, if the benefit requires informing others of his purpose and where he intends to go, then this is more complete than concealing it; for in making it known there are benefits: preparing its provisions, undertaking the matter with insight, and showing longing for this noble act of worship, as Musa said: ﴿I will not give up until I reach the meeting place of the two seas, or I will journey on for years﴾; and as the Prophet (ﷺ) informed his companions when he marched to Tabuk, stating his direction openly, although his habit was to use indirect speech; and that was in accordance with what benefits.

Among them: attributing evil and its causes to Satan, in the sense of enticement and adornment, although everything is by God's decree and determination, as in the statement of Musa's servant: ﴿And none caused me to forget it except Satan, that I should mention it﴾.

Among them: the permissibility of a person reporting what is part of the nature of the soul, such as weariness, hunger or thirst, when it is not in the manner of complaining bitterly and is truthful; as in Musa's statement: ﴿We have indeed suffered weariness from this journey of ours﴾.

Among them: the recommendation that a person's servant be clever, perceptive and shrewd, so that the matter he intends may be accomplished for him.

Among them: the recommendation that a person feed his servant from his own food, and that they eat together; for the apparent meaning of his words ﴿Bring us our morning meal﴾, attributing it to all of them, is that he and his servant both ate.

Among them: that help descends upon the servant according to his fulfilling what he is commanded, and that one who complies with God's command is helped in ways that others are not helped; as in His statement ﴿We have indeed suffered weariness from this journey of ours﴾, referring to the journey beyond the meeting place of the two seas. As for the first journey, they did not complain of weariness during it despite its length, because it was the true journey. As for the last one, it apparently lasted part of a day, because they lost the fish when they took refuge at the rock; so apparently they spent the night there, then they set out the next day, until when it came time for the morning meal, Musa said to his servant: ﴿Bring us our morning meal﴾; then he remembered that he had forgotten it at the place which was the end of his goal.

Among them: that this servant whom they met was not a prophet, but a righteous servant; for He described him with servanthood, and mentioned God's favor upon him with mercy and knowledge, and did not mention his messengership or prophethood; and had he been a prophet, that would have been mentioned as it was mentioned for others. As for his statement at the end of the story: ﴿And I did not do it of my own accord﴾, it does not indicate that he was a prophet, but indicates inspiration and being spoken to by God, as is the case for non-prophets, as God, exalted be He, said: ﴿And We inspired the mother of Musa: suckle him﴾, and ﴿Your Lord inspired the bee: take for yourself houses in the mountains﴾.

Among them: that knowledge which God teaches His servants is of two kinds: acquired knowledge, which the servant attains through his diligence and effort; and a kind of knowledge given directly from God (ladunni), which God bestows on whom He favors among His servants; as in His statement: ﴿And We taught him knowledge from Our presence﴾.

Among them: courtesy toward the teacher, and that the student addresses him in the gentlest manner; as in the words of Musa (peace be upon him): ﴿May I follow you on condition that you teach me of what you have been taught, as guidance?﴾. He phrased his speech in a manner of gentleness and consultation: whether you permit me in that or not. And his acknowledgment that he is learning from him, unlike the case of those who are rude or proud, who do not show the teacher their need for his knowledge, but claim that they cooperate with him, and may even think that they are teaching their teacher while being utterly ignorant. Humbling oneself before the teacher and showing one's need to be taught is among the most beneficial things for the student.

Among them: the humility of the superior person in learning from one who is below him; for Musa was without doubt superior to al-Khidr.

Among them: the learning of a superior scholar in a field in which he has not mastered from one who has mastered it, even if the latter is below him in knowledge by many degrees; for Musa (peace be upon him) was among the ulu al-'azm (steadfast resolute messengers), whom God granted and gave knowledge that He gave to no one else; but in this specific knowledge, al-Khidr had what Musa did not have. Therefore he eagerly sought to learn from him. On this basis, it is not appropriate for a jurist or hadith scholar who is deficient in the science of grammar (nahw), morphology (sarf), or similar disciplines to refrain from learning them from one who has mastered them, even if he himself is not a hadith scholar or jurist.

Among them: attributing knowledge and other virtues to God, the Exalted, acknowledging that, and thanking God for them; as in His statement ﴿that you teach me of what you have been taught﴾; that is, of what God, the Exalted, has taught you.

Among them: that beneficial knowledge is knowledge that guides to good. Every knowledge that contains guidance and direction to the path of good, and warning against the path of evil or a means to that, is beneficial knowledge. Anything beyond that is either harmful or has no benefit; as in His statement ﴿that you teach me of what you have been taught, as guidance﴾.

Among them: that whoever lacks the strength of patience in keeping company with a scholar and with knowledge, and lacks steadfastness in that, will lose much of the knowledge in proportion to his lack of patience. Whoever lacks patience does not attain knowledge, and whoever employs patience and persists in it attains through it every matter he strives for. This is shown by al-Khidr's statement, excusing himself to Musa by mentioning the obstacle that prevents Musa from learning from him: that he would not be able to remain patient with him.

Among them: that a major cause of attaining patience is a person's comprehensive knowledge and experience of the matter for which he has been commanded to be patient; otherwise, one who does not understand it, or does not understand its end, result, benefit or fruit, does not possess the cause of patience. This is shown by His statement ﴿And how can you have patience about that which you do not encompass in knowledge?﴾; so He made the reason for his lack of patience his failure to comprehend the matter in knowledge.

Among them: the command to be deliberate and careful, and not to rush to judge a thing until one knows what is intended by it and what its purpose is.

Among them: making future actions that depend on human choice conditional upon God's will, and that a person should not say of something: "I will do that in the future," except by saying "God willing."

Among them: that resolving to do something is not the same as doing it; for Musa said: ﴿You will find me, God willing, patient﴾.

Then he resolved to be patient, but he did not do so.

Among its lessons: when the teacher sees that it is in the student's interest to be restrained from beginning to ask about certain matters, so that the teacher is the one who brings him to them, then the teacher may do so, since benefit follows what is best. This applies, for example, when the student's understanding is limited, or when the teacher forbids him from probing into matters whose importance is less than others, or matters his mind cannot grasp, or when he asks a question that is not relevant to the subject under discussion.
